source.title: Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey Theory

accepted.question_text: For each positive integer r, what is the minimum Euclidean dimension n such that every partition, equivalently every r-coloring, of all points of Euclidean n-space into r parts contains the four vertices of a unit square in one part?

evidence.quote: if the points of Euclidean n-space are partitioned into r parts
the minimum value of n for which this is true depends on r is still not known

accepted.question_text: Let E^2 denote the Euclidean plane. A set X is monochromatic in a coloring if all points of a congruent copy of X receive the same color. For every non-equilateral triangle T, viewed as the set of its three vertices, must every 2-coloring of E^2 contain a monochromatic congruent copy of T?

evidence.quote: then we often say that E^N contains a monochromatic copy of X
Conjecture 1 For any non-equilateral triangle T

accepted.question_text: For every partition of the Euclidean plane E^2 into two color classes C1 and C2, is it true that one of the two classes contains congruent copies of every triangle, with at most one exceptional equilateral triangle that may fail to occur in either class?

evidence.quote: For any partition E^2 = C1 ∪ C2, every triangle occurs
with the possible exception of a single equilateral triangle

accepted.question_text: For every triangle T, must every 3-coloring of Euclidean three-space E^3 contain a monochromatic congruent copy of T?
accepted.context_brief: Triangles in three-space with three colors

evidence.quote: Conjecture 3 For any triangle T

accepted.question_text: For positive real numbers a and b, a degenerate triangle with side lengths a, b, and a+b is a collinear three-point configuration whose two smaller consecutive distances are a and b. It is known that, for every dimension n, Euclidean n-space E^n can be colored with 16 colors so that no monochromatic copy of any such degenerate triangle occurs. Can the constant 16 be reduced, and in particular is there a universal number r < 16, possibly r = 2, with the same avoidance property?

evidence.quote: E^n can be 16-colored to prevent the degenerate (a,b,a+b) triangle
Conjecture 4 The number 16 above can be reduced.

accepted.question_text: For each dimension n, determine the chromatic number χ(E^n), the least number of colors needed to color Euclidean n-space so that no two points at unit distance have the same color. In particular, determine χ(E^2), where the source records the classical bounds 4 ≤ χ(E^2) ≤ 7, and χ(E^3), where it records 6 ≤ χ(E^3) ≤ 15.

evidence.quote: called the chromatic number of E^n and is denoted by χ(E^n)
Even for n = 2, the value of χ is quite mysterious
The best bounds known for n = 3 are 6 ≤ χ(E^3) ≤ 15

accepted.question_text: Call a finite subset X of some Euclidean space Ramsey if, for every number of colors r, every sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space colored with r colors contains a monochromatic congruent copy of X. A necessary condition stated in the source is that any Ramsey set must lie on the surface of a sphere in some dimension; such a set is called spherical. Is every spherical finite set Ramsey?

evidence.quote: any Ramsey set must lie on the surface of a sphere
Conjecture 5 ($1000). Every spherical set is Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: Is every four-point subset of a circle Ramsey, meaning that for every number of colors r, all sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean spaces colored with r colors must contain a monochromatic congruent copy of that four-point circular set?

evidence.quote: An easier conjecture is this:
Every 4-point subset of a circle is Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: Frankl and Rödl define a finite set A to be super-Ramsey if, for sufficiently large N, there are subsets X of E^N of size less than c^N such that every subset Y of X with no copy of A has size less than |X|/(1+ε)^N, for some positive constants c and ε. Are the super-Ramsey finite sets exactly the spherical finite sets?

evidence.quote: Frankl and Rödl define the following stronger concept
the super-Ramsey sets are just the spherical sets

accepted.question_text: A finite set X is sphere-Ramsey if, for every number of colors r, there exist a dimension N and a radius ρ such that every r-coloring of the sphere S^N(ρ) contains a monochromatic congruent copy of X. If X is Ramsey in Euclidean space, must X also be sphere-Ramsey?

evidence.quote: We will say that X is sphere-Ramsey if for all r
Conjecture 7 ($1000). If X is Ramsey then X is sphere-Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: For edge colorings of line segments in Euclidean space, call a finite line-segment configuration E edge-Ramsey if, for every number of colors r, every sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space has the property that any r-coloring of its line segments contains a monochromatic copy of E. Is the edge set of a regular hexagon not edge-Ramsey?

evidence.quote: we will say that E is edge-Ramsey
Conjecture 8 The edge set of a regular hexagon is not edge-Ramsey.

accepted.question_text: Characterize all finite line-segment configurations E that are edge-Ramsey: those for which, for every number of colors r, every sufficiently high-dimensional Euclidean space has the property that any r-coloring of its line segments contains a monochromatic copy of E.

evidence.quote: given some fixed finite configuration E of line segments
(Big) Problem Characterize edge-Ramsey configurations

accepted.question_text: In asymmetric Euclidean Ramsey notation, E^N ->_2 (X1, X2) means that every 2-coloring of E^N contains either a congruent copy of X1 in color 1 or a congruent copy of X2 in color 2. Let P2 be a two-point set whose points are distance 1 apart. The source records a set T8 of eight points in E^2 for which E^2 does not arrow (P2, T8). Is there a set T with fewer than eight points in E^2 such that E^2 has a 2-coloring with no color-1 copy of P2 and no color-2 copy of T?

evidence.quote: we denote this by E^N ->_2 (X1, X2)
There is a set T8 of 8 points in E^2
It is not known if there are sets with fewer than 8 points

accepted.question_text: For every integer n, must every set of 2^(n-2)+1 points in the plane in general position, meaning no three points are collinear, contain n points that are the vertices of a convex n-gon?

evidence.quote: Any set of 2^{n-2} + 1 points in the plane in general position
must contain the vertices of a convex n-gon

accepted.question_text: Let N be the set of natural numbers. If A is a subset of N^2 such that the sum over all (x,y) in A of 1/(x^2 + y^2) diverges, must A contain the four vertices of an axes-parallel square?

evidence.quote: If A ⊆ N^2 with Σ 1/(x^2 + y^2) = ∞
A must contain the 4 vertices of an axes-parallel square

accepted.question_text: Let N be the set of natural numbers. If A is a subset of N and the reciprocal sum Σ_{a in A} 1/a diverges, must A contain arithmetic progressions of every finite length? The source also notes that it was not even known whether this hypothesis forces a 3-term arithmetic progression.

evidence.quote: If A ⊆ N satisfies Σ 1/a = ∞
then A must contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions
not even known if this hypothesis implies that A has a 3-term arithmetic progression

trace.notes: Original input was a zbMATH landing page. Local fetch of the web page was blocked by Cloudflare, so the zbMATH API was used as resolver metadata only. It identified zbMATH document 2112060 as Ron Graham, Open problems in Euclidean Ramsey theory, Geombinatorics 13(4), 165-177 (2004). A UCSD-hosted PDF with the matching title and author was downloaded and used as the readable primary source.

Mapped scanned PDF by page images. Sections: 1 Introduction; 2 Ramsey Sets; 3 Sphere-Ramsey Sets; 4 Edge-Ramsey Sets; 5 Variations; References. Definitions indexed: monochromatic congruent copy, r-Ramsey arrow notation, Ramsey set, chromatic number of E^n, spherical set, super-Ramsey set, sphere-Ramsey set, edge-Ramsey configuration, asymmetric Ramsey notation.
Introduction yielded the unit-square dimension problem, triangle Conjectures 1-4, and the chromatic-number problem for Euclidean spaces.
Ramsey Sets yielded spherical-set, four-point-circle, and super-Ramsey classification candidates.
Sphere-Ramsey Sets yielded the conjecture that every Ramsey set is sphere-Ramsey.
Edge-Ramsey Sets yielded the regular-hexagon conjecture and the broad problem of characterizing edge-Ramsey configurations.
Variations yielded the fewer-than-eight-point asymmetric Ramsey question and the three final prize conjectures.
